figure: Figure 1.1 — KV cache detail view (token -> append K/V -> stored K / stored V -> read for attention)
issue: The drawing does not encode the one-step delay between sampling a generated token and writing its K/V. The figure alone therefore supports an off-by-one reading that the caption explicitly forbids, and the caption's central distinction is carried entirely by prose rather than by the diagram.
evidence: Caption (printed p. 7): 'for a generated token, written when that token is next processed as input, one step after it is sampled: prompt-token K/V is written during prefill.' Figure labels: 'token1 / from prefill', 'token2 / first decode', 'token3 / second decode', '... token_n / nth decode', each with an identical arrow into the orange box 'append K/V per layer-head'. Nothing in the drawing distinguishes 'token sampled at step t' from 'token processed as input at step t+1'; the prefill token and the decode tokens are drawn with the same arrow semantics and the same box treatment. A reader scanning the figure can conclude that each decode step appends the K/V of the token it just sampled, which is wrong by one step.
acceptance_test: Redraw so write timing is legible without the caption: label the append arrows 'written during prefill' (token1) and 'written at step t+1' (token2, token3), or add a step axis / step counter to the token column. Acceptance: a reader shown only the figure (caption obscured) states correctly that a generated token's K/V is written one step after it is sampled, and that prompt-token K/V is written during prefill.

figure: Figure 1.1 — secondary annotations ('from prefill', 'first decode', 'second decode', 'nth decode', 'layer L . h1...h_h', 'next token q')
issue: The smallest in-figure annotations appear to fall at or below the 8 pt print floor, and they carry essential semantics (which token is which; which layer/head the stored tensors belong to; what the query is).
evidence: At 150 dpi the secondary annotation glyphs render at roughly 0.6-0.7x the x-height of the 10.5 pt body text set on the same page (compare 'not the expert count: GQA/MQA shrink the per-token KV width...' immediately below the caption). 'layer L . h1...h_h' and 'next token q' are the smallest and are the least redundant strings in the figure: they are the only place the reader learns the cache is indexed per (layer, head) and that the attention step consumes a query. The primary labels ('token1', 'append K/V', 'stored K - keys', 'read for attention') are visibly larger and legible.
acceptance_test: Measure the smallest annotation at 100% on the printed page, or extract font sizes from the figure source: every figure glyph, including 'layer L . h1...h_h' and 'next token q', must be >= 8 pt. If any is below, raise the figure's minimum type size and re-verify that the figure still fits the text block without shrinking the primary labels.

figure: Figure 1.1 — color coding of the store path vs. the read path
issue: The read path and the store path are distinguished by hue alone, and the hues used are close in luminance, so the distinction largely disappears in grayscale. The distinction survives only because both paths are text-labeled.
evidence: The 'store K' and 'store V' arrows are mid-gray; the 'read V' and 'read K' arrows and the 'read for attention' box are green; the 'stored K - keys' and 'stored V - values' boxes are lavender. A green of roughly (46,125,50) converts to a luminance near 93/255, and a mid-gray arrow near (100,100,100) converts to near 100/255 - a difference of about 3% of full scale, i.e. not perceptible. The lavender box border and the green box border likewise land within a few percent of each other in grayscale. The figure is therefore not self-explanatory in a grayscale print or for a reader with color-vision deficiency, except through the words 'store' and 'read'.
acceptance_test: Convert the figure to grayscale at 300 dpi and confirm that the read path is distinguishable from the store path without relying on hue. If it is not, differentiate by line style (e.g. solid store arrows, dashed read arrows) or by box shape, so that hue becomes redundant rather than load-bearing.

figure: Figure 1.1 — notation 'layer L . h1...h_h'
issue: Possible notation collision: 'h' is used here to index attention heads, while 'h' is a common symbol for hidden dimension elsewhere in transformer literature and possibly elsewhere in this manuscript. NOT VERIFIED against the rest of the book (only pages 27-28 were in this batch).
evidence: Figure boxes read 'layer L . h1...h_h'; the caption reads 'each enumerated per head (h1...h_h)'. If the manuscript elsewhere uses 'h' for hidden size (e.g. hidden state h, or a hidden dimension of 8,192 for the canonical dense model), the same glyph denotes two different quantities within one page, which is exactly the kind of drift a reader cannot resolve from context.
acceptance_test: Grep the manuscript for 'h' used as a hidden-dimension symbol and for 'h1...h_h' / 'h_h'. If both exist, rename the head index in Figure 1.1 and its caption (e.g. 'head 1...head H' or 'm1...m_H') and add the chosen symbol to the notation list. If 'h' is not used for hidden size anywhere, close this item with no change.

figure: Figure 1.1 — green box 'read for attention / next token q'
issue: The label conflates the query with the next token and leaves the query's origin unshown, so the box can be read as 'the next token's query is read out of the cache', which is false: the cache supplies K and V only; the query is produced by the projection of the token currently being processed.
evidence: The only two arrows entering the green box are labeled 'read V' (from 'stored V - values') and 'read K' (from 'stored K - keys'). The second line of the box label, 'next token q', sits directly beneath 'read for attention' with no arrow showing where q originates, and the figure has no arrow returning from the attention box to the token column, so the chain terminates without showing that the attention output produces the next token.
acceptance_test: Relabel the box to make the query's role explicit (e.g. 'attention over cached K, V / query q_t from current token') and add an arrow from the token column into the box labeled 'project to q', or a return arrow labeled 'produces next token'. Acceptance: no reader can describe the cache as supplying the query.

figure: Section 1.3 prose immediately above Table 1-1 (worked example)
issue: The worked example's stated token arithmetic is internally inconsistent: the printed operands do not sum to the printed total, and the operand contradicts the canonical scenario, the bullets below it, and Table 1-1 on the same page.
evidence: Printed text: 'If average request is ~2K input + ~300 output = 9.5K tokens per request'. 2K + 300 = 2.3K, not 9.5K. The canonical-scenario sentence two lines above reads 'prompt of ~1,200 tokens plus ~8K retrieved context (~9.2K prompt)'; the bullet below reads 'Input tokens/s: 9,200 tokens/req x 10 req/s = 92,000 tokens/s'; Table 1-1 on the same page lists 'input tokens / request ~9,200' with derivation '1,200 prompt + 8K context'. The only self-consistent reading is 9.2K + 300 = 9.5K, so the operand is wrong, not the total. (Note: at 150 dpi the operand glyphs are small; if the source string is in fact '~9.2K input' and the rendered page is correct, this finding is void - but the source must be checked, because a reader seeing '~2K input' alongside '= 9.5K' will conclude the book cannot do arithmetic.)
acceptance_test: Grep the source for '9.5K tokens per request' and confirm the preceding operand is '~9.2K input'. Then re-derive: 9,200 + 300 = 9,500; 9,200 x 10 = 92,000; 9,200 x 40 = 368,000; 9,200 / 300 = 30.7 (~30x). All four must hold on the printed page. If the source reads '~2K input', rewrite to '~9.2K input + ~300 output = 9.5K tokens per request'.

figure: Table 1-1 - Token throughput of the canonical workload (worked example, not reference)
issue: The table is split across the page boundary at the foot of printed page 8 with no closing rule visible; the continuation (presumably the tokens/s rows that the prose bullets compute) falls on printed page 9, which was not in this batch. A split table without a repeated header row is a publication-quality defect.
evidence: The last visible row on printed p. 8 is 'output tokens / request | ~300 | canonical scenario (Ch. 4, Table 4-2)', rendered flush to the bottom margin with no bottom rule, indicating the table continues. The header row ('metric | value | derivation') and the caption ('Table 1-1 - Token throughput of the canonical workload (worked example, not reference)') appear only above the split. The prose immediately preceding the table already states the derived rates (92,000 input tokens/s; 3,000 output tokens/s), so the reader is likely to encounter the table's rate rows only after the rates have been asserted in prose.
acceptance_test: Inspect printed page 9: the continuation must repeat the header row and carry a 'Table 1-1 (continued)' caption, or the table must be rebalanced so it fits on one page. Acceptance: a reader who turns to page 9 sees the header row before any data row.

figure: Table 1-1 - caption vs. tabulated quantity
issue: The caption names a rate ('Token throughput') while the rows visible on the page where the table begins are per-request token counts, not throughput. This is only a defect if the throughput rows are not in the table; if they are (on the continuation page), the caption is acceptable but the split still leaves the caption describing a quantity that is not on the page.
evidence: Caption: 'Table 1-1 - Token throughput of the canonical workload (worked example, not reference)'. Visible rows: 'input tokens / request ~9,200' and 'output tokens / request ~300'. The word 'throughput' conventionally denotes a rate (tokens/s), which is what the prose bullets compute but what the visible rows do not tabulate.
acceptance_test: After resolving TAB-1.1-03, confirm the caption names the quantities actually tabulated. If the table contains only per-request counts, retitle to 'Token counts per request in the canonical workload (worked example, not reference)'; if it contains both counts and rates, keep the caption but ensure the rate rows are not separated from the caption by a page break.

figure: Table 1-1 - 'derivation' column, row 'input tokens / request'
issue: The derivation cell states the same source twice in two different formats, and the duplication forces an unnecessary line wrap in a column that is otherwise short.
evidence: The cell reads, on two lines, 'canonical scenario (Ch. 4, Table 4-2)' and 'Table 4-2 (1,200 prompt + 8K context)'. The reference 'Table 4-2' appears twice; the second line's informational content is only the arithmetic decomposition '1,200 prompt + 8K context'. The adjacent row's derivation cell uses the single form 'canonical scenario (Ch. 4, Table 4-2)', so the table is internally inconsistent in how it cites the same source.
acceptance_test: Replace the cell with one line: 'canonical scenario (Ch. 4, Table 4-2): 1,200 prompt + 8K context'. Acceptance: the string 'Table 4-2' appears exactly once per derivation cell, and the row height is reduced to a single line.

figure: FIGURE 1.2 (p. 10) — caption, second paragraph
issue: The caption contains an unbalanced parenthesis and an orphaned clause, so the sentence that is supposed to define the KV cache's role cannot be parsed without the reader reconstructing the intended structure.
evidence: Printed text reads verbatim: "...and the KV cache is a persistent state — written (append) and read (read past K,V, the backward read arrow from the KV cache back to attention across steps — not a processing stage." The parenthesis opened after "read (" is never closed; the parenthetical mixes an arrow label ("read past K,V"), an appositive ("the backward read arrow from the KV cache back to attention"), and the temporal qualifier ("across steps"), and the closing em-dash clause "— not a processing stage" is left syntactically orphaned. This is the caption of the book's first figure and the sentence that establishes the single most consequential distinction in the chapter (cache = persistent state, not a processing stage).
acceptance_test: Rewrite so that every parenthesis balances and each clause has one owner, e.g.: "...and the KV cache is a persistent state — written (the 'append K,V' arrow) and read (the 'read past K,V' arrow, which returns past K/V to attention) across steps — not a processing stage." Verify by re-reading the caption aloud for grammatical closure and by confirming that no '(' remains unmatched in the caption source.

figure: FIGURE 1.2 — edge label on the Embedding → Attention arrow
issue: The forward edge from Embedding to Attention is labeled "attend", which misattributes the attention operation to the wrong edge and invites a reading that contradicts the caption's own insistence that the past-token read path is the backward arrow.
evidence: The Attention box's two sub-lines read "Q,K,V (this token)" and "vs. all past tokens". The only edge carrying past tokens is the green "read past K,V" arrow from KV Cache back into Attention. Labeling the Embedding→Attention edge "attend" therefore suggests that the attending happens on the forward edge, i.e. that the past tokens arrive with the embedding — which is exactly the misconception the caption spends a paragraph disarming ("the backward read arrow from the KV cache back to attention across steps"). The edge actually carries the current token's hidden state, from which Q (and the current token's K, V) are projected.
acceptance_test: Relabel the Embedding → Attention edge to name what it carries (e.g. "hidden state" or "Q from this token"), leaving "attend" as the operation described inside the Attention box. Confirm that after the change no edge label implies that past tokens enter via the forward path.

figure: FIGURE 1.2 — box sub-labels ("user prompt", "characters", "BPE, byte-level", "corpus-driven", "order = position", "ID to d-dim vector", "one vec/token", "Q,K,V (this token)", "vs. all past tokens", "read + write", "per layer × head")
issue: The box sub-labels appear to be set at roughly 65–75% of the caption's type size, which places them at or below the documented 8 pt print floor for figure in-text annotations. These are the labels that carry the figure's actual content (the per-box qualifiers), so they are the last thing that should be shrunk.
evidence: At 150 dpi the sub-label glyphs measure visibly smaller than the caption's body-size text on the same page (e.g. "user prompt" and "per layer × head" versus "Conceptually only: what is drawn is..."). If the caption is set at 9–10 pt, the sub-labels land at approximately 6–7.5 pt. NOTE: this is an estimate from the rendered page, not a measurement of the source font size — the exact value must be confirmed in the figure source or by measuring the built PDF at 100% zoom.
acceptance_test: Measure the rendered cap-height of the smallest annotation in Fig 1.2 in the built PDF at 100% zoom (or read the font size from the figure source). If any annotation is below 8 pt, raise the sub-label size to at least 8 pt and re-check that the box widths still accommodate the longest strings ("ID to d-dim vector", "per layer × head") without clipping or extra wrapping.

figure: FIGURE 1.2 — box fills/borders and the "read past K,V" arrow
issue: Color is used for two incompatible purposes at once, and there is no legend, so the reader cannot infer what the palette encodes. In grayscale the six box fills collapse to near-identical light grays and the palette carries no information at all.
evidence: Green/teal is used both as the fill+border of the Tokenizer and Embedding boxes (i.e. as a "token-space" category) and as the sole distinguishing color of the "read past K,V" arrow (i.e. as "the backward read"). The remaining forward arrows ("split", "emit", "lookup", "attend", "append K,V") are all neutral gray. The six box fills (gray, mint, peach, mint, blue, lavender) all convert to approximately the same light gray value in grayscale, and the borders all convert to similar mid-gray, so in a black-and-white print the only surviving distinction is the bold box title. The figure remains interpretable in grayscale because every box is titled, but the color grouping (Tokenizer/Embedding as a pair) is lost and the green arrow's special status survives only as "slightly darker arrow".
acceptance_test: Either (a) re-color the "read past K,V" arrow with a hue not used by any box, or (b) add a one-line legend stating what the palette encodes, and confirm that the figure remains fully interpretable when converted to grayscale (all six boxes still distinguishable by title, and the backward arrow still identifiable as the only non-gray arrow).

figure: FIGURE 1.2 — left half (Text → Tokenizer → Token IDs → Embedding) vs. right half (Attention → KV Cache)
issue: The diagram silently mixes prompt-level operations with per-token operations without marking where one level ends and the other begins, while the caption describes the whole thing as "the one-token-to-state construction".
evidence: "split", "emit", and "lookup" are prompt-level operations performed once over the whole input (the Text box is labeled "user prompt / characters"). "attend", "append K,V", and "read past K,V" are per-token, per-step operations. The figure title ("How a token travels: text → tokenizer → IDs → embedding → attention → KV cache") therefore describes a chain that changes cardinality halfway across, and the caption's "one-token-to-state construction" gloss does not resolve it. A reader can plausibly infer that the whole prompt is embedded once and then attended as a unit, or that the tokenizer emits one token at a time into the embedding stage.
acceptance_test: Mark the level boundary in the figure — e.g. a light bracket or a small annotation under the Token IDs → Embedding edge reading "per prompt" and under the Attention → KV Cache edge reading "per token, per step" — or state the distinction in one clause of the caption. Confirm that a reader can answer "which of these boxes run once per request and which run once per generated token?" from the figure alone.

figure: Reference to "the figure" in the paragraph beginning "One detail the figure makes explicit is when a token's K/V enters the cache."
issue: The paragraph attributes an explicitness to an unnamed "the figure" that Fig 1.2 does not in fact possess, and the ambiguity is resolvable only by guessing which of the two figures in scope is meant.
evidence: Printed p. 14 opens: "One detail the figure makes explicit is when a token's K/V enters the cache." The paragraph then explains the input-vs-sampled distinction ("A KV token's K/V therefore enters the cache on the step in which it is the input, not on the step in which it is sampled") and cites "the green initialize path in Fig 2.1". Fig 1.2 (printed p. 10) shows a single token in isolation and therefore cannot show the input-vs-output distinction at all; that distinction requires the step-to-step loop, i.e. Fig 2.1 (printed pp. 11–13). The nearest preceding figure reference on the page is Fig 1.2, so "the figure" is genuinely ambiguous.
acceptance_test: Replace "the figure" with the explicit figure number ("Fig 2.1") in the first sentence of that paragraph, and confirm that the sentence's claim — that the figure makes the cache-entry timing explicit — is true of the figure actually cited.

figure: FIG 1.2 (p. 10) vs. Fig 2.1 (pp. 11–13, not in this batch)
issue: Possible cross-figure color-semantics collision: green appears in Fig 1.2 as the "read past K,V" (backward read) arrow, while printed p. 14 refers to a "green initialize path in Fig 2.1". If both are green, the same hue encodes two unrelated meanings across two consecutive figures.
evidence: Fig 1.2 uses a distinctly green arrow for the backward read from KV Cache to Attention. Printed p. 14 states: "that first token is the input that seeds the decode loop (the green initialize path in Fig 2.1)". NOT VERIFIED: Fig 2.1 falls on printed pp. 11–13 and was not rendered in this batch, so I cannot confirm its actual color usage. This finding is conditional on that inspection.
acceptance_test: Render and inspect Fig 2.1 (printed pp. 11–13). If its initialize path is also green, either recolor one of the two so that a given hue carries one meaning across both figures, or add a shared legend for the two figures. If the hues are already distinct, close this item with no change.

figure: FIGURE 2.1 — canonical end-to-end inference pipeline
issue: The green 'initialize' path crosses the two black KV-cache arrows ('read' downward, 'append' upward) without any junction or bridge marker. The green horizontal segment runs at the vertical level just above the DECODE band's top edge, spanning from the figure's right margin to the 'previous token' box; the black read/append arrows run vertically from the bottom of the PERSISTENT KV CACHE box down to the top of the decode band's 'transformer' box, so they intersect that horizontal segment. In a diagram whose only color-coded distinction is the green path, an unmarked crossing of a green line over two black arrows invites the reader to read a connection (e.g. 'the initialize path feeds the cache read') that the caption explicitly denies.
evidence: Rendered page 35: the green horizontal segment at approximately y=345 px (image is ~580 px wide for 8.5 in, i.e. ~68 px/in) spans x≈122–478; the black read arrow (x≈278) and append arrow (x≈300) both span y≈300–352 and therefore cross it. No crossing marker, no 'no connection' bridge, no directional break. The caption's only disambiguation is the sentence 'The initialize path (labelled initialize) seeds the loop with the first sampled token', which is prose rescue for a visual ambiguity.
acceptance_test: Re-render the figure at 300 dpi and confirm the two crossings persist. Then re-route the initialize path so it does not intersect the read/append arrows — e.g. run it below the KV-cache box and enter 'previous token' from the left, or run it along the far right and drop into 'previous token' from above-left of the band. If a crossing is retained, add explicit bridge markers at both intersections and state in the caption that crossings are not junctions. Acceptance: a grayscale 300-dpi render shows zero unmarked line-line crossings.

figure: FIGURE 2.1 — annotation 'conceptual per-step per-layer cache I/O'
issue: The italic gray annotation 'conceptual per-step per-layer cache I/O' has three independent defects: (a) it is the smallest and lightest text in the figure (light-gray italic, visibly smaller than the other arrow labels 'populate', 'read', 'append', 'initialize', 'loop'), so it is the first element to disappear at print size or in a low-quality grayscale reproduction; (b) it is placed far to the right of the read/append arrows it annotates (roughly 50–170 px away), immediately adjacent to the green initialize path, so it reads as a label for the green path or for the 'logits + sampling' box rather than for the cache I/O arrows; (c) its baseline sits only a few pixels above the green initialize horizontal segment, so the two nearly touch. The annotation is also redundant: the caption already states 'each step reads the cached K/V, appends the new K/V'.
evidence: Rendered page 35: annotation occupies approximately x=350–450, y=330–343, in light-gray italic; the green horizontal segment is at y≈345–347 across the same x-range; the read/append arrows it describes are at x≈278 and x≈300. Contrast of the annotation is visibly lower than every other label in the figure.
acceptance_test: Either delete the annotation (the caption carries the same fact) or (i) move it immediately adjacent to the read/append arrows, (ii) set it in the same black roman face and size as the other arrow labels (>= 8 pt at final print size), and (iii) verify >= 3 mm clearance from the green initialize path. Acceptance: a 300-dpi grayscale render shows the annotation at >= 8 pt, in black, with no element within 3 mm, and positioned so that its referent is unambiguous without the caption.

figure: FIGURE 2.1 — PERSISTENT KV CACHE box vs. the two process bands
issue: The figure uses one visual grammar for two different kinds of object. The PREFILL band, the DECODE band, and the PERSISTENT KV CACHE are all drawn as bordered rounded rectangles with the same fill family, and the KV cache is placed vertically between the two bands with arrows entering and leaving it. A reader scanning the figure can therefore read it as a three-stage pipeline — PREFILL -> KV CACHE -> DECODE — i.e. as a processing stage rather than as persistent state. That is precisely the misconception the caption spends two sentences disarming ('conceptual groupings for teaching, not runtime components: a real serving stack has per-layer, per-request KV ...'). The figure should carry that distinction in its own visual grammar rather than delegating it entirely to prose. The visual hierarchy compounds the risk: the KV cache is the largest, boldest, most centrally placed element, so the figure's emphasis points at the cache rather than at the two phases the caption calls out as the TTFT and TPOT determinants.
evidence: Rendered page 35: PREFILL band (x≈85–470, y≈143–195), PERSISTENT KV CACHE (x≈160–405, y≈235–290, bold uppercase label), DECODE band (x≈85–470, y≈350–405) — all three share the same rounded-rectangle-with-border treatment; the cache is the only element with a bold, letter-spaced, all-caps label.
acceptance_test: Give the PERSISTENT KV CACHE a distinct visual treatment (storage glyph, distinct fill/hatch, or a different outline weight) so that it cannot be parsed as a third processing stage, and verify in a grayscale render that the store is distinguishable from the two process bands without relying on color. Acceptance: a reader shown only the figure (no caption) describes the KV cache as state that persists across the two phases, not as a pipeline stage.

figure: FIGURE 2.1 — caption, final clause
issue: The caption's closing sentence appears garbled in the built PDF. As rendered it reads: '...not runtime components: a real serving stack has per-layer, per-request KV prefills "prefill band" object. [ILLUSTRATIVE conceptual]'. The clause 'per-request KV prefills "prefill band" object' is not grammatical, the quoted phrase '"prefill band"' appears nowhere else in the caption, and the sentence has no predicate. This is the caption of the book's canonical pipeline figure — the one figure that Chapter 2 and later chapters refer back to — so a broken sentence here is a reader-facing defect in the most-reused visual artifact in the book. It is also the sentence that carries the figure's most important caveat (the bands and the single cache box are teaching abstractions, not runtime components), so the caveat is currently not reliably legible.
evidence: Rendered page 35, caption lines 6–8: 'The two bands and the single PERSISTENT KV CACHE box are conceptual groupings for teaching, not runtime components: a real serving stack has per-layer, per-request KV prefills "prefill band" object. [ILLUSTRATIVE conceptual]'.
acceptance_test: Extract the caption from the built PDF text layer (pdftotext -f 35 -l 35) and from the .tex source. If the string 'per-request KV prefills "prefill band" object' is present in either, rewrite the closing sentence to a grammatical form that preserves both the caveat and the label, e.g. '...not runtime components: a real serving stack holds per-layer, per-request KV caches, and the "prefill band" is a teaching abstraction.' Acceptance: the caption's final sentence has a subject and a predicate, the quoted phrase '"prefill band"' is either defined or removed, and the caveat survives verbatim in meaning. NOTE: this finding is based on the rendered page only; the source text was not inspected in this pass.

figure: FIGURE 2.1 — caption color sentence
issue: The caption states 'Color is figure-local decoration — each box is tinted.' Both halves are inaccurate as rendered: the inner boxes are white/unfilled with thin borders (they are not tinted), and the green 'initialize' arrow is not decoration — it is the figure's only color-coded distinction, separating the one-shot initialization path from the steady-state loop path. A reader who accepts the caption's blanket statement may conclude that the green carries no information and that the initialize/loop distinction rests on the labels alone, which is not the design intent.
evidence: Rendered page 35: all inner boxes (prompt, tokens + positions, transformer, logits + sampling, first token, previous token, token + position, next token) render as white fills with thin gray borders; the only saturated color in the figure is the 'initialize' arrow and its label.
acceptance_test: Check the .tex source for the box fill definitions. If the boxes are untinted, delete 'each box is tinted' and replace the sentence with something like 'Color distinguishes the one-shot initialize path from the steady-state loop path; all other elements are monochrome.' Acceptance: the caption's color statement is true of the rendered figure and does not assert that color is uninformative.

figure: FIGURE 2.1 — absence of a scale/emphasis qualifier
issue: The figure encodes no relative cost, and the caption's disclaimer covers only 'not runtime components', not 'not to scale'. The two bands are drawn at equal visual weight and the KV cache is drawn larger and more prominently than either band, so a reader can infer either that prefill and decode cost the same, or that the KV cache is the dominant resource. The caption asserts the opposite emphasis ('PREFILL ... is the dominant contributor to TTFT'; 'DECODE ... measured by TPOT'). The figure and the caption therefore disagree in emphasis without the figure disclaiming it.
evidence: Rendered page 35: PREFILL band and DECODE band are drawn with identical box sizes and identical styling; the PERSISTENT KV CACHE box is ~245 px wide and ~55 px tall with a bold label, visually the dominant element; no qualifier about scale appears in the caption.
acceptance_test: Add an explicit 'not to scale' qualifier to the caption, and/or annotate the two bands with the metric each one drives ('dominant TTFT contributor' on PREFILL, 'dominant TPOT contributor' on DECODE) so that the figure's emphasis matches the caption's claims without asserting a universal compute-bound/bandwidth-bound regime. Acceptance: the figure cannot be read as implying equal cost for the two phases or as implying the KV cache dominates runtime cost.

figure: FIGURE 2.1 — green initialize path routing
issue: The green initialize path's vertical segment runs immediately outside the right edge of both process bands (roughly 8 px at the rendered scale, i.e. on the order of 0.1 in or less at print size). The line therefore reads as a band boundary or as a bracket belonging to the bands rather than as a separate connector, and it is the segment that carries the figure's only color-coded distinction.
evidence: Rendered page 35: the green vertical segment is at x≈478; the PREFILL and DECODE band rectangles both terminate at x≈470.
acceptance_test: Re-route the initialize path with >= 3 mm clearance from the band outlines (or route it on the left side of the figure, where the 'loop' path already runs, with the two paths separated vertically). Acceptance: in a 300-dpi grayscale render the green path is unambiguously a connector and not a band edge.

figure: FIGURE 2.1 — page placement
issue: Printed page 15 carries only the figure and its caption; roughly the bottom quarter of the page (on the order of 2 inches) is blank, and the following section does not begin on the page. For a book whose page budget is tight and whose figures are the primary teaching artifacts, this is wasted page real estate and it also means the reader meets the figure with no adjacent prose to prime the labels.
evidence: Rendered page 35: figure occupies y≈120–460, caption y≈485–600, page bottom margin begins at y≈620 with the footer at y≈735; no body text follows the caption on the page.
acceptance_test: Reflow so that the figure, its caption, and the opening prose of the following section share the page, or move the figure to a page where it can be followed by text. Acceptance: no trailing blank block of more than ~1 inch below the last element on the page.

figure: FIGURE 2.2 — Prefill and decode: two regimes split by the roofline ridge
issue: The roofline is drawn as a single rising line with no horizontal plateau. The compute-bound region (blue, horizontal hatch) is shaded all the way to the top of the plot (1e+15 FLOP/s), but the figure's own annotation states the machine's ceiling is 989 TFLOPS (9.89e14). A reader therefore sees the compute-bound regime as permitting performance up to 1e15 FLOP/s, i.e. above the stated hardware peak. The classic roofline shape (rising ridge + flat ceiling) is missing, and the flat ceiling is the single most important visual fact about the compute-bound regime.
evidence: Rendered page 43: the black ridge line terminates at the top frame near x≈295; to its right the blue 'compute-bound' fill continues to the 1e+15 gridline with no horizontal boundary. The annotation 'H100 SXM, BF16 dense: 989 TFLOPS peak, 3.35 TB/s HBM3 → ridge at 295 FLOP/byte' fixes the ceiling at 9.89e14 FLOP/s, and the floating '989 TFLOPS' text sits at the top of the plot where the plateau should be. The caption's claim that 'prefill sits in the compute-bound regime' is therefore drawn against a region whose upper bound contradicts the stated peak.
acceptance_test: Redraw so that a horizontal ceiling line at 9.89e14 FLOP/s runs from the ridge (AI≈295) to the right edge of the plot, with the compute-bound hatch filling only below that line; attach the '989 TFLOPS peak (BF16 dense)' label to that line. Re-render at 150 dpi and confirm (a) no blue hatch above 9.89e14, (b) the ceiling line is visually continuous with the rising ridge, (c) the prefill marker lies below the ceiling.

figure: FIGURE 2.2 — roofline ridge line
issue: The drawn ridge line is geometrically inconsistent with the stated hardware bandwidth. On a log–log roofline the ridge must satisfy y = AI × BW, i.e. slope exactly 1 in log–log, passing through (AI=1, y=3.35e12) and (AI=295, y=9.89e14). As rendered, the line's lower-left endpoint sits at approximately y≈1e12 at AI=1 and reaches 1e15 at AI≈295, which implies BW≈1e12 B/s — a factor of ~3.4 below the annotated 3.35 TB/s. The figure is the book's central quantitative device for the prefill/decode regime split, and a reader who checks the arithmetic against the drawn line will find it does not hold.
evidence: Rendered page 43: black line lower-left endpoint ≈ (x=1 tick, y=1e+12 gridline); upper-right endpoint ≈ (x≈295, y=1e+15). Independently: 989e12 / 3.35e12 = 295.2 FLOP/byte (ridge AI, consistent with the annotation), and the ridge height at AI=1 must be 3.35e12 FLOP/s, i.e. ~0.52 decade above the 1e+12 gridline. The drawn endpoint is ~0.5 decade below that.
acceptance_test: Regenerate the ridge from the annotated constants (y = AI × 3.35e12, capped at 9.89e14) rather than hand-placing endpoints, then verify on the rendered page that the line passes through (1, 3.35e12) and (295, 9.89e14) to within the line width, and that its log–log slope is 1.

figure: FIGURE 2.2 — 'prefill' marker (x-position) vs caption and prose
issue: Three different values are in play for the canonical prefill arithmetic intensity, and they do not agree: (a) the caption says the canonical prefill point is '~2K FLOP/byte'; (b) the printed prose on the facing page (printed p.20) repeats 'the canonical prefill point ~2K FLOP/byte'; (c) the figure's 'prefill' triangle is drawn at roughly 4×10^3 FLOP/byte. Worse, ~2K is itself inconsistent with the canonical scenario the book states (70B-class dense model, 1,200 + 8K = 9,200 input tokens): for a dense model, prefill arithmetic intensity ≈ 2·N_params·N_tok / (2·N_params + KV bytes) ≈ N_tok, i.e. ≈9×10^3 FLOP/byte for a 9.2K-token prefill (≈7.8×10^3 if the 24 GB of KV writes are included; ≈9.1×10^3 with attention FLOPs added). A ~2K FLOP/byte prefill corresponds to roughly a 2,000-token prefill, not the canonical 9.2K.
evidence: Rendered page 43: 'prefill' triangle at x ≈ 4×10^3 (between the 1000 and 10000 ticks, ~0.6 decade past 1000). Caption: 'the canonical prefill point ~2K FLOP/byte'. Printed p.20 (PDF p.40): 'the canonical prefill point ~2K FLOP/byte'. Canonical scenario (printed p.20): 70B-class dense, FP16, 1,200 + 8K retrieved context = 9.2K input tokens. Derivation: FLOPs = 2 × 70e9 × 9200 = 1.288e15; bytes ≈ 140 GB weights + 24.1 GB KV write (9200 × 2.62 MB/token) + ~1 GB activations ≈ 165 GB; AI ≈ 7.8e3 FLOP/byte (≈9.2e3 ignoring KV writes).
acceptance_test: Fix one canonical prefill arithmetic-intensity value, state it once in the caption, and place the marker at exactly that x-coordinate (2×10^3 → 0.30 decade past the 1000 tick; 9.2×10^3 → 0.96 decade). Then re-derive it in the text from the canonical scenario (AI ≈ N_prefill_tokens for a dense model) and confirm the prose on printed p.20, the caption, and the marker agree to the stated rounding. If the canonical scenario's prefill length is intended to be ~2K tokens, change the scenario instead and propagate.

figure: FIGURE 2.2 — 'roofline ridge ~295' label vs unlabeled black line
issue: The red label 'roofline ridge ~295' sits above the dashed vertical line, but 'roofline ridge' is the natural name for the black diagonal line (the roofline), which is itself unlabeled. A reader can plausibly read the red label as naming the black line, in which case the black line would be claimed to be at AI≈295 — i.e. a vertical line — which is nonsense. The two lines carry two different meanings (a performance ceiling vs. an intensity location) and neither the caption nor the figure disambiguates them.
evidence: Rendered page 43: red text 'roofline ridge ~295' positioned above the plot at the dashed line's x; the black diagonal line has no text label anywhere in the figure or caption. Caption refers to 'the roofline ridge' and 'the ~295 ridge' without saying which drawn element is which.
acceptance_test: Label the black line directly (e.g. 'roofline: y = AI × 3.35 TB/s, capped at 989 TFLOPS') and rename the red annotation to 'ridge AI ≈ 295 FLOP/byte' with a short leader to the dashed line; add one clause to the caption stating that the solid line is the roofline and the dashed line marks the ridge's arithmetic intensity.

figure: FIGURE 2.2 — bottom-left annotation 'H100 SXM, BF16 dense: 989 TFLOPS peak, 3.35 TB/s HBM3 → ridge at 295 FLOP/byte'
issue: This annotation is set in small type directly on top of the diagonally hatched peach memory-bound fill, immediately above the x-axis and beside the '1e+11' tick label. It also restates, redundantly and in a second location, the two facts already given by the floating '989 TFLOPS' label and the 'roofline ridge ~295' label.

acceptance_test: Move the hardware-constants annotation out of the hatched region — either below the x-axis as a figure note or into the caption — and delete whichever of the two in-figure labels becomes redundant once the ceiling line is drawn (see FIG-2.2-01). Confirm at 150 dpi that the text sits on a plain background with no hatch behind it.

figure: FIGURE 2.2 — italic note 'markers = regime, not measured MFU (real kernels run below the roof)'
issue: This is the figure's most important epistemic caveat — it tells the reader that the two markers are regime indicators, not measurements — yet it is rendered in small, light-gray italic type on the hatched peach fill in the upper-left of the plot. It is the least legible text in the figure and it carries the heaviest interpretive load. The caveat is also not repeated in the caption, where it would be read reliably.
evidence: Rendered page 43: two-line italic gray note at approximately x∈[165,300] px, y≈170–185 px, over the diagonal hatch; visibly lower contrast and smaller than every other annotation. The caption discusses regimes and operating points but does not state that the markers' vertical positions are not measured MFU.

figure: FIGURE 2.2 — 'prefill' marker vertical position
issue: The prefill triangle is placed at roughly 5×10^14 FLOP/s, i.e. about half the 989 TFLOPS ceiling. That vertical placement silently encodes a specific assumed MFU (~50%), which the caption does not license and the figure's own note disclaims. figure: FIGURE 2.2 — color semantics and grayscale behavior
issue: Red carries two unrelated meanings in this figure: the 'decode' marker and the dashed ridge-AI line. In grayscale the decode marker (solid red circle) sits on the peach memory-bound fill and loses contrast against it, and the red dashed line becomes a mid-gray dashed line that could be confused with a gridline. The figure survives grayscale only because shape (circle vs triangle) and dash pattern carry the distinctions; the color assignments themselves do not.
evidence: Rendered page 43: red circle on peach/orange hatched fill; red dashed vertical line; blue triangle on blue hatched fill; blue 'compute-bound' text on blue hatch. Grayscale separation depends entirely on shape and hatch direction (diagonal vs horizontal), which is adequate but not by design.
acceptance_test: Convert the figure to grayscale and confirm that (a) the decode marker is distinguishable from the memory-bound fill, (b) the dashed ridge line is distinguishable from gridlines, (c) the two region labels remain legible on their hatched fills. If any fails, add shape/dash redundancy (e.g. hollow vs filled markers, a distinct dash pattern for the ridge line) rather than relying on hue.

figure: FIGURE 2.2 — y-axis label 'attainable performance (FLOP/s)'
issue: The y-axis is labeled 'attainable performance', which invites the reading that the plotted values are achievable performance figures, while the figure's own note says the markers are not measured MFU and the caption calls the whole thing '[ILLUSTRATIVE]'. The axis is in fact a roofline ceiling, not an attainable-performance measurement.
evidence: Rendered page 43: y-axis label 'attainable performance (FLOP/s)'; figure note 'markers = regime, not measured MFU (real kernels run below the roof)'; caption '[ILLUSTRATIVE] conceptual roofline developed in Ch 8'.
acceptance_test: Rename the y-axis to 'roofline ceiling (FLOP/s)' (or 'performance bound (FLOP/s)') and confirm the caption and axis label use the same term for the same quantity.
